title: [suite à La "Longue Marche" à travers la théorie de Galois..., pages 650 bis à 787, dont table des matières] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: this page continues §3 ('Les groupes ... D_N^*') of the sequel to La Longue Marche, ms. p. 673. On the previous page Grothendieck introduces a group scheme over S_0 that encodes quantities mu in G_m, nu', nu'' in G_a and nu_2, nu_3 in {0,1} subject to (63). The integers 2, 3, 4, 6 and the choice N = 12 point to SL_2(Z) = Z/4 *_{Z/2} Z/6, the abelianization Z/12, and the arithmetic of M_{1,1}. That link is my inference.

He defines D_N as the pushout of the constant group Z_{S_0} along multiplication by N, with Z -> G_a. Equivalently, D_N is the quotient (Z_{S_0} x G_a)/Z, where k maps to (Nk, -k). It sits in an extension 0 -> G_a -> D_N -> (Z/N)_{S_0} -> 0. Its sections are written n + N[lambda], with addition (67a).

This page:
- (68) puts a multiplication on D_N: (n + N[lambda])(n' + N[lambda']) = nn' + N[n lambda' + n' lambda + (N) lambda lambda']. Heuristically, N[lambda] stands for 'N times lambda', so the formula is just distributivity.
- He checks that the product is compatible with the identification (67b) and is biadditive, commutative and associative, with unit 1 + N[0]. So D_N =: O_N is a commutative ring scheme over S_0.

He then generalizes:
- Let A be a unital associative Z-algebra and J a two-sided ideal that is free of finite type as a Z-module. Put B = A/J, with extension (69) 0 -> J -> A -> B -> 0.
- Let J_ be the vector group J ⊗ G_a. Form the pushout A_[N] := (A_{S_0} x J_)/J, where J is embedded by lambda -> (lambda, -lambda) (70).
- Give A_{S_0} x J_ the 'half-direct product' ring structure (a, x)(a', x') = (aa', ax' + xa' + xx'). It is not the square-zero semidirect product, because J_ keeps its own multiplication.
- The antidiagonal copy of J is a two-sided ideal. Check: (a, x)(lambda, -lambda) = (a lambda, -a lambda), and (lambda, -lambda)(lambda', -lambda') = (lambda lambda', -lambda lambda').
- Hence A_[N] is a ring scheme, with an extension 0 -> J_ -> A_[N] -> B_{S_0} -> 0 of ring schemes (71, next page).

Taking units (72-74, next page) gives 1 -> (1 + J_)^* -> A_[N]^* -> B^*_{S_0} -> 1. For A = Z, J = NZ this is 1 -> (1 + N G_a)^* -> O_N^* -> (Z/N)^*_{S_0} -> 1. Here (1 + N G_a)^* is the group scheme of lambda with 1 + N lambda invertible, under the law lambda + lambda' + N lambda lambda'. This is the 'dilatation' of G_m that deforms G_a to G_m (Waterhouse–Weisfeiler, Sekiguchi–Oort–Suwa G^(N)).

Geometrically:
- Over S_0[1/N], the map n + N[lambda] -> n + N lambda identifies O_N with G_a as ring schemes.
- In characteristics p dividing N, O_N acquires a constant Z/N quotient.

The purpose is apparently to build the group scheme D_N^* (N = 12) needed to describe some abelianized pi_1 / Picard-type invariant over arbitrary bases S_0.
errors: (68) as written, N[n lambda' + n' lambda + lambda lambda'], is not compatible with the identification (n, lambda) ~ (n + N, lambda - 1) if lambda is a section of G_a. Compatibility forces the last term to be N lambda lambda'. The formula is right only if [lambda] is read as a section of J_ = NZ ⊗ G_a, which is the general version on the same page with product xx'. This is a notational slip, not a conceptual error.

As transcribed on the previous page, (67b) reads 'n + N[lambda] = n' + N[lambda'] iff n + N lambda = n' + N lambda' in Gamma G_a'. That criterion is only correct where N is invertible. The intended relation is: there is a locally constant integer k with n' = n + Nk and lambda' = lambda - k. This may be a transcription issue.
(70) writes A_N for what is called A_[N] elsewhere; this is a notational inconsistency only.
J free of finite type is needed so that J_ = J ⊗ G_a is a representable vector group scheme. This is used implicitly and is fine.

ideas.what: Ring scheme O_N = pushout of the constant ring Z_{S_0} along Z --N--> G_a, extension of (Z/N)_{S_0} by G_a, isomorphic to G_a away from N
ideas.modern_name: pushout/'dilatation' ring scheme; ring-scheme analogue of Néron-type dilatations
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure; related group-scheme constructions are due to Waterhouse–Weisfeiler (1980) and Sekiguchi–Oort–Suwa (1989)

ideas.what: General construction A_[N] from a Z-algebra A and an ideal J free of finite type: half-direct product ring A ⋉ J_ with product (a,x)(a',x') = (aa', ax' + xa' + xx'), modulo antidiagonal J
ideas.modern_name: pushout of ring schemes / constant ring glued with vector-ring scheme

ideas.what: Unit group extension 1 -> (1 + N G_a)^* -> O_N^* -> (Z/N)^* -> 1; the kernel is the group scheme x + y + Nxy
ideas.modern_name: group schemes G^(lambda) deforming G_a to G_m

missed.claim: Grothendieck builds a ring scheme over an arbitrary base whose unit group packages, at once, the constant (Z/N)^* (N = 12) and the Sekiguchi–Oort–Suwa-type deformation 1 + N G_a of G_a to G_m. This apparently serves to describe an abelianized fundamental-group / Picard-type invariant of the elliptic modular tower (2, 3, 4, 6, 12) uniformly over Z. That links the Z/12 of SL_2(Z)^ab and Pic(M_{1,1}) (later Mumford; Fulton–Olsson over general bases) with these group schemes. I know of no such ring-scheme formulation in the literature.
missed.quote: on trouve bien une structure d'anneau sur A_[N] ... (74) 1 -> (1+NZ)^* -> O_N^* -> (Z/N Z)^*_{S_0} -> 1
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It may give an integral, base-independent group-scheme model of the 'Z/12' phenomena of M_{1,1} (Picard group, Dedekind eta, Delta^{1/12}). It connects to work on Pic of moduli stacks over arbitrary bases and on G_a–G_m degenerations.

deep.surprise_reason: The algebra itself is elementary: pushout ring schemes and dilated multiplicative groups. Its use to build an integral group scheme D_12^* tied to the SL_2(Z)/M_{1,1} Z/12 story is unpublished and somewhat original, but the page shows only the routine ring-structure verification.
transcription_corrections: (68) last term: the image reads 'λλ'' but mathematically it should be Nλλ' under the N[λ] convention (or λ read in J_).
In (70) the quotient is written A_N (without brackets) in the image; same object as A_[N].
'A_{S_0}·J (produit semi-direct)': the dot denotes the semi-direct product A_{S_0} ⋉ J_; the crossed-out '(A)_{S_0}·NB ≠' is correctly marked deleted.
'J qui soit Z-module libre de t.f.': 'Z-module' is inserted between 'soit' and 'libre'.
